hub.title: Knowledge base: file formats, encodings, time and money math explained — cv.cm
hub.description: Clear, sourced explanations of HEIC, JPG vs PNG vs WebP, EXIF, DPI, Base64, UTF-8, URL encoding, hashes, UUIDs, Unix time, ISO 8601, time zones, APR vs APY and margin vs markup.
hub.lede: Short, sourced explanations of the formats, codes and numbers you meet every day. Each article answers the question first, then explains why, with links to the standards and to a free tool that runs in your browser.
about: Tutorials on cv.cm show how to get a job done. These articles explain what is going on underneath: why a photo is HEIC, why a PDF is 40 MB, why a password with four random words beats one with symbols.
Every article is checked against the published standard or official documentation listed under Sources, and dated so you can see when it was last reviewed.

faq.q: Who writes these articles?
faq.a: The cv.cm team writes them and checks each fact against the standards and official documentation listed at the end of every article.

faq.q: Can I use the tools mentioned here for free?
faq.a: Yes. The linked tools are free, need no account and process files in your browser.

faq.q: How is a knowledge article different from a tutorial?
faq.a: A tutorial walks through one task step by step. A knowledge article explains the idea behind it, such as how a format or a formula works, so you can make your own decisions.

codeHub.title: Coding tutorials: programming languages, design patterns and algorithms — cv.cm
codeHub.description: Free one-page tutorials for Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, Go, Rust and more, all 23 design patterns, and core data structures and algorithms, with code.
codeHub.lede: Learn a programming language, a design pattern or an algorithm on one page. Each tutorial answers the question first, then shows working code, the common mistakes and the official references.
about: Language tutorials take you from installing the tools and printing Hello, world to functions, collections, error handling and a small complete program. Pattern pages explain the problem each Gang of Four pattern solves, with a TypeScript example and when not to use it. Data structure and algorithm pages trace an example step by step, give Python code and state the time and space complexity.
Code samples are short and runnable as shown, and every page links to the language documentation, standard or original source it was checked against.

faq.q: Which programming language should I learn first?
faq.a: For most beginners Python or JavaScript: both have simple syntax, huge communities and run everywhere. Pick JavaScript for websites, Python for data, automation and general programming.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything to follow the tutorials?
faq.a: Each language tutorial starts with how to install the official tools and run your first program. Pattern and algorithm pages use TypeScript and Python, which you can run locally or in any online playground.

faq.q: Are these tutorials free?
faq.a: Yes. Every tutorial is free to read with no account, and the code samples may be reused in your own projects.

faq.q: What is the difference between data structures and algorithms?
faq.a: A data structure is a way to store data, such as an array, hash table or tree. An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem, such as sorting or finding a shortest path, and its speed often depends on the data structure it uses.

aiHub.title: AI tutorials: prompts, AI images and video, LLMs explained — cv.cm
aiHub.description: Free, sourced AI guides: how LLMs and diffusion models work, image and video prompts, camera moves, AI short videos for TikTok and Shorts, and AI copyright.
aiHub.lede: Learn how generative AI works and how to get good results from it. Each guide answers the question first, then shows the method with real prompts and examples, the common mistakes and the official sources.
about: The basics explain what large language models and diffusion models actually do, why they hallucinate and what tokens and context windows are. The prompt guides give reusable formulas for text, image and video prompts, with weak and strong versions side by side. The image, video and audio guides walk through each workflow from the first prompt to a finished file, and say where the tools still fail.

The guides are model-agnostic, so the methods work in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Kling, Veo and similar tools. Legal pages cite the official texts and are general information, not legal advice. Several guides link to cv.cm's free AI tools, which run in your browser without uploading your files.

faq.q: Where should a beginner start with AI?
faq.a: Read what generative AI is and how LLMs work, then the prompt writing basics. Those three pages explain most of what you need to get useful answers from any chatbot or image generator.

faq.q: How do I make AI short videos for TikTok, Reels or Shorts?
faq.a: Start with the guide to making AI videos, then the short video workflow. The AI short videos group covers scripts and hooks, voiceover, captions, platform sizes, editing, lip sync, music and dance videos.

faq.q: Do these tutorials depend on one AI tool?
faq.a: No. They teach methods that work across tools. Where a step depends on a product, the guide says so and describes the general option to look for.

faq.q: Can I use AI-generated images and videos commercially?
faq.a: Often yes, but it depends on the tool's license and terms, the law where you publish, and whether the output copies someone else's work or likeness. The copyright and labeling guides list what to check.

faq.q: Are the cv.cm AI tools free?
faq.a: Yes. The AI image generator, photo to video, background remover, upscaler and speech to text tools are free and run on your own device, so your files are not uploaded.

photoHub.title: Photography tutorials: camera settings, posing, wedding photos — cv.cm
photoHub.description: Free photography guides for camera and phone: aperture, shutter speed, ISO, composition, golden hour, posing, solo bridal and pre-wedding shoots, night and moon photos.
photoHub.lede: Take better photos with a camera or a phone. Each guide answers the question first, then gives starting settings, step-by-step methods, shot and pose lists, the common mistakes and how to fix them.
about: The camera settings guides explain the exposure triangle and each of its parts: aperture and background blur, shutter speed and motion, ISO and noise, plus white balance and focal length. Composition and light covers the rule of thirds, leading lines and framing, golden hour and shooting into the light. The portrait guides cover posing, directing people, selfies and photographing yourself with a tripod and timer.

The wedding guides plan a solo bridal shoot, a pose list for brides and a couple's pre-wedding shoot, with shot lists, settings for a white dress and checklists. Every guide gives steps for phones as well as cameras, cites camera and phone makers' official guides, and links to cv.cm's free browser tools such as the portrait camera simulator, crop and collage.

faq.q: Where should a beginner start with photography?
faq.a: Start with the exposure triangle, then the rule of thirds and golden hour. Those three guides explain most of the difference between a snapshot and a good photo, on a camera or a phone.

faq.q: How do I take wedding photos of just one person?
faq.a: Read the solo bridal photoshoot guide. It covers choosing between a studio, a photographer, a friend or a self-shot session, a planning checklist, a shot list, settings for a white dress and posing in a gown.

faq.q: Can I learn these settings without a camera?
faq.a: Yes. cv.cm's portrait camera simulator lets you change aperture, shutter speed, ISO and lens on simulated sitters and see the blur, motion and noise change, in your browser.

faq.q: Do the guides work for phone photos?
faq.a: Yes. Each guide says what to do on a phone: tap to focus, the exposure slider, locking focus and exposure, the grid, portrait and night modes, and which lens to use.

faq.q: Are these photography tutorials free?
faq.a: Yes. All guides and the linked cv.cm tools are free, and the tools run in your browser without uploading your photos.

massageHub.title: Self-massage tutorials: acupressure points, techniques — cv.cm
massageHub.description: Free self-massage guides: massage techniques, pressure points for headaches and eye strain, a foot reflexology chart, neck, back and foot massage, gua sha and massage guns.
massageHub.lede: Learn to massage yourself and the people close to you, safely. Each guide answers the question first, then shows where to press, how hard and for how long, a timed routine, what the evidence says and when to see a doctor instead.
about: The basics explain the main strokes, how much pressure to use and how long to spend on each area, and list when not to massage at all. The acupressure guides locate the most used points with bone landmarks and finger-widths, using the standard WHO point names, with short routines for tension headaches and tired eyes. The body guides cover feet, hands, neck and shoulders, the back, the face and the scalp.

The tool guides show how to use a gua sha stone, a massage gun, a foam roller and a tennis ball, and where never to use them. These guides are for relaxation and everyday self-care, not medical advice: each one says plainly what the research does and does not show, cites health agencies and peer-reviewed studies, and lists the warning signs that need a doctor.

faq.q: Where should a beginner start with self-massage?
faq.a: Start with how to massage, which covers the basic strokes and pressure levels, then read when not to massage. After that, pick the guide for the area that feels tight, such as the neck and shoulders.

faq.q: Do pressure points really work?
faq.a: Many people find pressing them relaxing. Research is limited and mixed: the best evidence is for the PC6 point on the wrist and nausea. Each guide says what the studies found and does not promise results.

faq.q: Is self-massage safe?
faq.a: For most healthy adults, gentle to moderate self-massage is safe. Avoid broken skin, fresh injuries, a swollen and painful calf, and deep pressure if you take blood thinners. Ask a doctor first if you are pregnant or have a medical condition.

faq.q: How long should I massage each area?
faq.a: One to three minutes per area, or 30 to 60 seconds per pressure point, is enough for most self-care routines. A timer helps you keep the pressure short and steady.

faq.q: Are these massage tutorials free?
faq.a: Yes. All guides and the linked cv.cm timers are free and work in your browser.
